case_info.scenario: A 61-year-old man presented to the otolaryngology clinic with a 2-month history of progressive hoarseness, dysphagia, odynophagia, and persistent globus sensation. He denied weight loss, fever, night sweats, cough, or hemoptysis. He had a history of coronary artery disease with prior coronary artery bypass grafting, peripheral vascular disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and ulcerative colitis. He reported no immunosuppressive therapy. He quit smoking 8 months prior after a 35–pack-year history and consumed alcohol infrequently. He denied recent travel, exposure to tuberculosis, or prior radiation to the head and neck. On physical examination, there were no palpable cervical lymph nodes or oropharyngeal abnormalities. Flexible laryngoscopy revealed a fibrinous, ulcerative lesion on the laryngeal surface of the epiglottis with surrounding edema and preserved bilateral vocal cord mobility. Given concern for cancer, the patient underwent direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Examination under anesthesia confirmed irregular mucosa with fibrinous exudate localized to the epiglottis. Histopathology results revealed necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells (Figure, A). Grocott methenamine silver stain highlighted narrow-based budding yeast (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Acutely inflamed, denuded laryngeal squamous mucosa with submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation (original magnification ×100). B, Biopsy demonstrating oval yeast forms consistent withHistoplasma capsulatum(arrowheads) measuring 2 to 4 μm in diameter with narrow-based budding (original magnification ×400).
case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. case_info.explanation: Laryngeal histoplasmosis is a rare extrapulmonary manifestation ofHistoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys. While histoplasmosis typically presents as a self-limited pulmonary illness, it may disseminate and affect extrapulmonary organs, including the larynx, even in immunocompetent individuals.1In this case, a man with no overt immunosuppression developed ulcerative supraglottic disease mimicking cancer, ultimately diagnosed by fungal staining on biopsy. Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. In cases where immunosuppression cannot be reversed, long-term suppressive therapy may be necessary.8,9 This patient received a 2-week course of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B followed by a prolonged course of oral amphotericin B, as recommended by the infectious team. He also experienced 2 transient ischemic attacks during hospitalization, likely from a septic origin, and began anticoagulation with warfarin. His hoarseness and odynophagia improved considerably within 1 month. At 3-month follow-up, he remained symptom free. The initial delay in diagnosis underscores the importance of including fungal infections in the differential diagnosis of ulcerative laryngeal lesions, particularly in endemic areas. Laryngeal histoplasmosis is an important clinical mimic of squamous cell carcinoma and TB, and early biopsy with fungal staining is critical for accurate diagnosis. Prompt antifungal therapy can prevent complications such as airway obstruction, systemic dissemination, or unnecessary oncologic intervention. This case reinforces the need for clinicians to maintain suspicion for histoplasmosis in patients with chronic hoarseness and supraglottic lesions, even in the absence of overt immunosuppression.

Endoscopic features of laryngeal histoplasmosis can closely resemble squamous cell carcinoma, with ulcerative lesions, irregular mucosa, or masslike findings localized to the epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, or vocal cords.2The overlap in appearance frequently leads to initial diagnostic concern for cancer, particularly in older adults with a history of tobacco use.3,4However, histopathologic evaluation remains the criterion standard for diagnosis. Histology results typically reveal necrotizing and nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and fungal organisms.5,6Grocott methenamine silver or periodic acid–Schiff staining identifies the characteristic small, oval intracellular yeasts ofH capsulatum. In this case, the biopsy lacked dysplasia or neoplasia but demonstrated abundant submucosal nonnecrotizing granulomatous inflammation and multinucleated giant cell formation with fungal organisms consistent withH capsulatum. A serum histoplasma antigen level was then obtained and returned positive at 1.95 ng/mL, supporting the diagnosis and prompting antifungal therapy. Alternative considerations include laryngeal tuberculosis (TB), which may also present with hoarseness, mucosal ulceration, and granulomatous inflammation. However, TB is identified by acid-fast bacilli on staining or culture.4In this patient, no acid-fast bacilli were found, and fungal organisms were clearly demonstrated. Chronic laryngitis, another consideration in those who smoke, does not typically cause ulceration or granulomas and lacks fungal or mycobacterial organisms.1 Imaging studies are generally nonspecific but may support the extent of involvement. In this case, imaging was not diagnostic. The patient’s location in the Ohio River Valley served as an epidemiologic clue. Inhalation of microconidia from contaminated soil, often associated with bird or bat droppings, is the primary route of exposure.3While disseminated disease is more common in immunocompromised patients, it may also occur in older or chronically ill individuals without overt immunodeficiency. The treatment of laryngeal histoplasmosis is guided by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. For moderate to severe disease, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends liposomal amphotericin B at 3.0 mg/kg/d for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by oral itraconazole at 200 mg twice daily for at least 12 months.7For mild to moderate cases, itraconazole may be sufficient alone. You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 62-year-old Japanese man was diagnosed with submandibular salivary duct carcinoma (T4bN3cM0 according to Union for International Cancer Control, 8th edition). He had alcohol use disorder with facial flushing after small amounts of alcohol, suggestive of aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) deficiency—a common genetic polymorphism in East Asian populations. He underwent right neck dissection with skin resection, reconstruction using a pectoralis major flap, and adjuvant radiotherapy (66 Gy). He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. Laboratory testing at that time showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 101.4 μm3(to convert to femtoliters, multiply by 1), and vitamin B12supplementation was initiated. In this clinical context, his sensory-dominant polyneuropathy was suspected to be related to chronic alcohol use and vitamin B12/folate deficiency. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), performed to evaluate for structural causes of neurologic symptoms, revealed multiple hypointense lesions on T1-weighted images in the thoracolumbar spine (Figure 1A); similar findings were observed on T2-weighted imaging (image not shown). The corresponding CT image demonstrated mild hyperdensity with ill-defined margins without cortical destruction (Figure 1B). Given his oncologic history and the imaging findings, a CT-guided biopsy of the signal alteration in the T12 vertebral body was performed by an orthopedic spine surgeon for definitive diagnosis.
